notes:
I could only partly finish this research, so some gaps remain. I ran out of searches before I could find any netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org or oca.org pages, or any Lutheran, Anglican or Pentecostal sites. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter. The only Catholic source I found is the Haydock note on v. 3, and my last attempt to load a page failed.

**Background (whole chapter)**
- Chapter 8 continues the prophecy of chapter 7 and runs on to 9:7. In chapter 7 God promised Ahaz that the Aram–Ephraim alliance would not defeat Judah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_8_commentary
- Wesley's outline: Syria and Israel fall to Assyria (vv. 1–4); Judah is afflicted (vv. 5–8); God is a sanctuary to the godly and a stone of stumbling to the wicked (vv. 14–15); people must wait on God, not consult necromancers (vv. 16–22). https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-isaiah/

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the name means "speed to the spoil, hurry to the plunder." Writing with "a man's pen" meant the message was public and plain enough for anyone to read. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Constable: the Hebrew word means a large flat surface that could be posted like a placard. Citing John Martin, he says soldiers shouted these words while plundering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html
- Calvin: each time the name was spoken it reminded people that Israel and Syria would be destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/8-1.html
- Clarke offers a more allegorical reading: the large scroll stands for Judea, and the four words for how few people would be left there. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/8-1.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: God named two witnesses so the word would be legally established, as in Deuteronomy 19:15. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Constable: the witnesses confirmed the date of the prophecy. Uriah was probably the high priest who built Ahaz's altar copied from Damascus (2 Kings 16:10–16). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html

**v. 3: Who was the "prophetess"? (readings differ)**
- Wesley: Isaiah's own wife, called a prophetess because she was a prophet's wife. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-8.html
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel, close to Pentecostal views on prophecy): she may have been a prophet in her own right, like Miriam, Deborah, Huldah or Anna. Or she may simply have been the prophet's wife, whose "prophecy" was the birth of this son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown: perhaps the same "virgin" as 7:14, who meanwhile became Isaiah's second wife. Even so, they say Immanuel and this son are different children. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_008.cfm
- Gill: Rashi thought the child was Immanuel, but Gill disagrees because the names and the mothers differ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/8-3.htm
- The Geneva Study Bible (Calvinist) says this happened in a vision. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/8-3.html Another commentator on Bible Hub disagrees with Calvin's vision view and says the passage reads as a literal birth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/8-3.htm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** the prophetess is either the Blessed Virgin Mary (citing St. Chrysostom) or Isaiah's wife. The son got a name different from Emmanuel so the two would not be confused. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/8-3.html

**v. 4**
- Wesley: a child can say "father" and "mother" within about two years, which fits 7:16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-8.html
- Constable: Assyria (Tiglath-pileser III) carried off the wealth of Damascus and Samaria in 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html
- Guzik: this is the same as the near meaning of the Immanuel sign in chapter 7, but given more publicly and plainly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/

**v. 6: Who is "this people"? (readings differ)**
- Wesley: the people of Israel (the north), who were pleased with their own king and with their ally Rezin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/8.htm
- Constable: Judah, who rejected God's faithful provision (the Shiloah channel from the Gihon spring). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html
- Precept Austin: rejecting the gentle waters really meant rejecting God himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_8_commentary

**v. 7**
- Guzik: Israel's small but adequate streams are contrasted with Assyria's huge, uncontrolled rivers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Constable: Assyria came because God sent it, not because its gods were stronger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html

**v. 8: "up to the neck" and "O Immanuel"**
- Guzik: Judah would be flooded but not drowned. Sennacherib took Judah's fortified cities (2 Kings 18:13), but Jerusalem survived. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Constable: the invasion came in 701 BC. "Immanuel" refers both to the child of 7:14 and to Israel as a whole. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html
- Wesley: the land is called Immanuel's because the Messiah would be born there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/8.htm
- Ironside: the phrase literally means the land of Palestine, though Christians may rightly use it in a spiritual sense too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-8.html
- **NET Bible note (modern scholarship, quoted on Precept Austin):** calling on Immanuel here is ironic, since God is present in judgment. The note gives several reasons to think Immanuel and Maher-shalal-hash-baz were the same child. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_8_commentary

**vv. 9–10: Who are the "peoples," and who is "us"? (readings differ)**
- Wesley: the peoples are the Syrians and Israelites, and anyone else who plots against Immanuel's land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-8.html
- Guzik: the "us" in "God is with us" could be the Assyrians, as God's tool of judgment, or the prophet himself. The phrase also echoes the name Immanuel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Calvin: having named Immanuel, Isaiah turns his mind to Christ and taunts the enemies as if they were already beaten. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom13/calcom13.xv.i.html
- Precept Austin (dispensational): these verses foreshadow the end of the age, when all nations come against Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60611

**vv. 11–13**
- Wesley: "strong hand" means unusually forceful inspiration. Isaiah is not to agree to Judah's alliance with Assyria. To "sanctify" the Lord means trusting his promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/8.htm
- Wesley notes that 1 Peter 3:14 quotes vv. 12–13 word for word from the Greek Old Testament. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-peter-3.html
- Guzik: fear God, not plots and threats. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/

**vv. 14–15: Stone of stumbling (main point of Protestant difference)**
- Shared reading: Guzik says the New Testament applies these verses to Jesus (1 Peter 2:6–8). Since Isaiah says the stone is the LORD of hosts, this is strong evidence that Jesus is God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- **Reformed / Calvinist:** The Geneva note says God will defend "his elect, and reject all the rest." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/8-14.htm Calvin warns that even many who call themselves Christians stumble at Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/8-14.html Piper, on 1 Peter 2:8 (which quotes v. 14), says Peter means that even the stumbling was something people were "appointed" to. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/why-god-laid-a-stone-of-stumbling
- **Wesleyan / Arminian:** Wesley stresses that "many" means "not all," because a remnant remains, and that people fell because the Jews rejected the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-8.html Ellicott (Anglican) adds that the fall is "not necessarily final." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/8-14.htm
- **Catholic:** catholic.com notes that Peter himself quotes Isaiah 8:13–14 to call Jesus both rock and stumbling stone. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/st-peter-rock-or-stumbling-stone

**v. 16: What does sealing mean? (readings differ)**
- Wesley: "testimony" and "law" both mean God's word, especially its teaching about the Messiah. It is sealed so that it will surely be fulfilled, yet hidden from unbelievers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-8.html
- Matthew Henry: Scripture is sealed, so nothing may be added to it or taken from it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/8-19.html
- Precept Austin, citing Oswalt: one view is that Isaiah's prophecies were stored with his disciples, to be published once events proved him right. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_8_commentary

**v. 17**
- Guzik: waiting on the Lord means close, active attention, like a waiter serving a table. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Constable: God seemed silent and inactive at the time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html

**v. 18**
- The names carry the message: Maher-shalal-hash-baz (judgment), Shear-jashub ("a remnant shall return") and Isaiah ("salvation is of the LORD"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-8/
- Wesley: Isaiah speaks literally of himself but "mystically" of Christ, which is why Hebrews 2:13 applies the words to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-8.html
- Delitzsch (quoted by Constable): Hebrews can quote these as Jesus' words because the Spirit of Jesus was in Isaiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html

**v. 19**
- Constable: when faith is lost, superstition grows. It is ironic to ask the dead about the living. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html
- Pulpit Commentary: in crises Israel was often tempted to turn to the occult, as with Saul and the medium of Endor, and Manasseh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/8-19.htm
- Debated application: Guzik says this verse also shows that praying to the saints is foolish. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Isa/Isa-8.cfm I did not find a Catholic answer to this.

**v. 20: How should it be translated? (readings differ)**
- Calvin, Barnes and Spurgeon: Scripture is the test for every claim of revelation. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/isaiah/8-20.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/8-20.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/8-20.html
- Pulpit Commentary and the Cambridge Bible translate it differently: in their deep trouble the people will *surely* take up this cry, but too late. The Cambridge Bible adds that the Hebrew is too unclear for any translation to be certain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/8-20.htm
- Ellicott: the verse is only "remotely" a call to study Scripture in general. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/8-20.htm
- Constable: "testimony" may mean royal tradition, which was reliable but not inspired. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html

**vv. 21–22**
- Wesley: they curse their king for his foolish advice and their "god," meaning their idol. Finding no help from heaven, they look down to the earth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/8.htm
- Constable: wherever they turn, frustration meets them (compare Revelation 16:11). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-8.html
- Guzik: leaving God's word for mediums leads to darkness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Isa/Isa-8.cfm
